analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing employees and consumers to sign away their right to sue before a dispute happens.
analysis.headline: The Arbitration Fairness Act of 2015, backed by 87 House members, sat in the Judiciary Committee for the rest of the Congress and never got a hearing, a markup, or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Almost every employment contract, credit card agreement, and user agreement now includes a clause requiring disputes to be settled by a private arbitrator instead of a judge and jury, and blocking class-action lawsuits. The bill would make those pre-dispute arbitration clauses unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, so workers and consumers could take their cases to court. Companies could still offer arbitration after a dispute arises, if the person agrees voluntarily. The bill never moved past its committee assignment.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers with mandatory arbitration in their employment contracts, consumers with arbitration clauses in credit card, telecom, and service agreements, and people with civil rights or antitrust claims who would regain the right to a day in court and the ability to band together in class actions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Workers and consumers with arbitration clauses

how_it_helps.text: The bill declares that no predispute arbitration agreement is valid or enforceable if it requires arbitration of an employment, consumer, antitrust, or civil rights dispute [S2] [S3].
It puts a court, not an arbitrator, in charge of deciding whether an arbitration agreement is valid, closing a common loophole where the arbitrator decides their own authority [S2] [S3].
The bill's findings state that most consumers and employees have little or no meaningful choice whether to submit claims to arbitration, and are often unaware they gave up their rights [S3].
Arbitration would remain available when consent is truly voluntary and happens after a dispute arises [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Corporations that write mandatory arbitration clauses into employment and consumer contracts would face more lawsuits, jury trials, and class actions, and would lose the private, low-appeal forum that currently resolves disputes on their own terms.

drawbacks.text: Business groups argue that arbitration is faster and cheaper for individuals than court, and that class actions mainly enrich lawyers while providing little recovery to class members; this bill would push many disputes into litigation. No hearing was held to weigh this in the record.
The bill covers a very broad range of disputes, which would substantially increase the caseload of federal courts, a cost honest supporters would acknowledge.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade-off is real: forced arbitration is often quicker and cheaper for an individual case, but it is also private, rarely appealable, and typically strips away the class-action mechanism that makes small-dollar claims economically possible at all. The bill does not ban arbitration, only arbitration imposed before a dispute exists, which preserves voluntary arbitration while restoring access to court for claims individuals rarely bring alone. The bigger practical weakness is not design but process: the bill was never debated, so its scope was never tested or narrowed.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Judiciary Committee and a subcommittee, where it stayed until the Congress ended, never getting a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on April 29, 2015 by Rep. Hank Johnson with 66 original cosponsors, all Democrats, and referred to the House Judiciary Committee [S3] [S5].
On June 26, 2015 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Regulatory Reform, Commercial and Antitrust Law [S5].
It gained 86 cosponsors over the session, all Democrats, and no further action was taken before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Companies that rely on mandatory arbitration clauses to keep disputes out of court and block class actions are better off, since the rules they operate under stayed exactly as they were. Workers and consumers gained nothing.

for.name: Hank Johnson
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and led the effort to end forced arbitration in employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes.

for.name: 86 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill over the course of the session.

against.name: Bob Goodlatte
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a committee markup or brought it to the floor during the two-year session.

sides.party_line_note: All 87 supporters in the House, the sponsor and 86 cosponsors, were Democrats; not a single Republican signed on, and with Republicans controlling the House and the Judiciary Committee, the bill never advanced.

industries.industry: Employers and consumer-facing corporations using mandatory arbitration clauses
industries.note: These companies would lose the ability to require employees and customers to arbitrate disputes privately and to block class-action lawsuits, which would expose them to more jury trials and larger collective liability. Their interest in keeping the clauses runs directly against workers' and consumers' access to court.

A large share of the private arbitration business comes from contractually mandatory consumer and employment cases; the bill would remove that pipeline while leaving voluntary post-dispute arbitration in place. Their revenue depends on the practice the bill would end.
Restoring access to court and class actions would expand the market for attorneys representing workers and consumers. Their gain comes alongside the public's restored access to court.
